items.title: Newton's First Law
items.body: A body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by a resultant force. Inertia.

items.title: Newton's Second Law
items.body: \(F=ma\) where \(F\) is resultant force (N), \(m\) is mass (kg), \(a\) is acceleration (m/s²).

items.title: Newton's Third Law
items.body: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Forces occur in equal pairs on different bodies.

items.title: Connected Particles
items.body: Particles connected by strings over pulleys: apply \(F=ma\) to each particle separately, then solve simultaneously.

items.title: Acceleration on Slopes
items.body: Net force along slope \(=mg\sin\alpha - F_{friction}\). Apply \(F=ma\) to find acceleration.

body.en: N1: A body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a net force. N2: \(F=ma\) (net force = mass × acceleration). N3: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. For connected particles (e.g. Atwood's machine), consider each particle separately; the tension \(T\) is the same throughout an inextensible string over a smooth pulley.

label.en: ● Deep Conceptual Intuition — Newton'\(s\) Laws of Motion

body.en: Proportional Invariance, Linear Structure & Quantitative Modeling: Across Cambridge International AS Level (9709 Paper 1 / Paper 4 / Paper 5), multi-step problems reduce to identifying invariant quantities—constant rates of change \(m = \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\), conservation of total work/mass, or linear system rank conditions. A two-variable linear system \(a_1 x + b_1 y = c_1\), \(a_2 x + b_2 y = c_2\) has a unique intersection if \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} \ne \dfrac{b_1}{b_2}\), no solution (parallel lines) if \(\dfrac{a_1}{a_2} = \dfrac{b_1}{b_2} \ne \dfrac{c_1}{c_2}\), and infinitely many solutions if all three ratios coincide.

body.en:
Separate equations for connected bodies: Never attempt to guess internal forces in one step. Always write \(\Sigma F = ma\) separately for each particle in its direction of motion. Adding the equations cancels the internal tension \(T\) and yields \(a\) immediately.

Assumptions and vocabulary: Cambridge papers frequently ask for the physical significance of modeling assumptions: 'Light' means string/pulley mass is negligible; 'Inextensible' means accelerations of both particles have the same magnitude; 'Smooth' means tension \(T\) is uniform across both sides.

Force exerted on the pulley: For two vertical hanging strings, the total downward force on the pulley is \(2T\). If one string is horizontal along a table and the other hangs vertically, the resultant force on the pulley is \(\sqrt{T^2 + T^2} = T\sqrt{2}\) at \(45^\circ\).

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Newton'\(s\) Laws of Motion)

body.en:
Why Successive Multipliers & Harmonic Average Speed Work: If a quantity \(Q_0\) undergoes a percentage change \(p\%\) followed by \(q\%\), the compound multiplier is the product of individual scale factors:

\[ Q_{\text{final}} = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p}{100}\right)\!\left(1 + \frac{q}{100}\right) = Q_0\left(1 + \frac{p + q}{100} + \frac{pq}{10000}\right) \]

Notice the cross term \(\dfrac{pq}{10000}\): an increase of \(p\%\) followed by a decrease of \(p\%\) yields \(Q_0\bigl(1 - (p/100)^2\bigr) < Q_0\). Similarly, traveling equal distance \(d\) at speeds \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) takes total time \(T = \frac{d}{v_1} + \frac{d}{v_2}\), so average speed is the harmonic mean \(v_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{2d}{d/v_1 + d/v_2} = \dfrac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\).

label.en: Worked example — Single particle on a surface

body.en:
A force of 30 N acts on a 6 kg box on a rough horizontal surface (\(\mu=0.3\), \(g=10\) m/s²). Find the acceleration.

\[R=mg=60\text{ N},\quad F_\text{friction}=0.3\times60=18\text{ N}.\]\[F_\text{net}=30-18=12\text{ N},\quad a=\frac{12}{6}=2\text{ m/s}^2.\]

label.en: Worked example — Connected particles over a pulley

body.en:
Two particles of mass 4 kg and 6 kg are connected by a light inextensible string over a smooth pulley. Find the acceleration and the tension in the string (\(g=10\) m/s²).

Taking down as positive for the 6 kg particle:

\[6g-T=6a,\quad T-4g=4a.\]\[\text{Adding: }2g=10a\Rightarrow a=2\text{ m/s}^2,\quad T=4(10+2)=48\text{ N}.\]

label.en: Worked Example \(C\) — Newton'\(s\) Laws of Motion (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): In the plane, the line \( 22z + 20y = 440 \) intersects the axes at points \( G \) and \( H \). Find the sum of intercepts \( M \) of \( 22z + 20y = 440 \).

Step-by-Step Solution: **Mark Scheme (CAIE / Edexcel Grading Steps):** - **Step 1 (Method & Formulation):** Identify the required geometric/algebraic relationship from the diagram and substitute the given values. **[M1]** - **Step 2 (Derivation & Calculation):** The intercepts are \( 20 \) and \( 22 \), whose sum is \( 20 + 22 = 42 \). **[M1]** - **Step 3 (Final Accuracy):** Verified exact result: 42. **[A1]**

label.en: Worked Example \(D\) — Newton'\(s\) Laws of Motion (Medium Application)

body.en:
Problem (Medium): A particle of mass 8 kg is moving under the action of a net force \( \mathbf{F} \) N. The acceleration of the particle, \( \mathbf{a} \) m/s\(^2\), is given by the vector \( \mathbf{a} = \begin{pmatrix} 2t - 4 \\ t^2 - 9 \end{pmatrix} \) for \( t \ge 0 \), where \( t \) is the time in seconds. Find the magnitude of the net force acting on the particle at \( t = 3 \) seconds.

Step-by-Step Solution: At \( t = 3 \) seconds, the acceleration vector is: \[ \mathbf{a}(3) = \begin{pmatrix} 2(3) - 4 \\ 3^2 - 9 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\text{ m/s}^2. \] By Newton's Second Law, \( \mathbf{F}(3) = m\mathbf{a}(3) = 8\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 16 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}\text{ N} \), so the magnitude of the net force is \( |\mathbf{F}(3)| = 16\text{ N} \).

rows.en: The \(25\%\) reduction applies to the larger base \(1.25 Q_0\), not \(Q_0\).
Dividing by a negative number reverses order on the real number line.
Flip the inequality symbol whenever multiplying or dividing by a negative: \(x < -4\).
Computing round-trip average speed as \(\frac{v_1 + v_2}{2}\)
Time spent at the slower speed is longer than time spent at the faster speed.
Use total distance over total time: \(v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}\).

label.en: ▲ Exam Pacing & Verification Strategy — Newton'\(s\) Laws of Motion

body.en: High-Speed Exam Shortcut (Cambridge International AS Level (9709 Paper 1 / Paper 4 / Paper 5)): When a linear system asks for a combined expression like \(3x + 3y\) rather than \(x\) and \(y\) individually, add or subtract the two equations directly before isolating either variable—this often yields the target expression in a single step.

question.en: Two particles \(P\) of mass \(3\text{ kg}\) and \(Q\) of mass \(5\text{ kg}\) are connected by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth fixed pulley. The system is held at rest and released. Taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\): (a) find the acceleration \(a\) of the system, (b) calculate the tension \(T\) in the string, (c) find the force exerted by the string on the pulley.

solution.en:
(a) Write \(F = ma\) for each particle in its direction of motion:
For \(Q\) (moving downwards): \[5g - T = 5a\] For \(P\) (moving upwards): \[T - 3g = 3a\] Add the equations: \[2g = 8a \Rightarrow a = \dfrac{2(9.8)}{8} = 2.45\text{ m/s}^2\] (b) Substitute \(a\) into the equation for \(P\): \[T = 3g + 3a = 3(9.8 + 2.45) = 3(12.25) = 36.75\text{ N} \approx 36.8\text{ N}\] (c) The pulley supports two vertical segments of string with tension \(T\), so the total downward force on the pulley is: \[F_{\text{pulley}} = 2T = 2(36.75) = 73.5\text{ N}\]

hints.en: (a) Write \(F = ma\) for each particle in its direction of motion: For \(Q\) (moving downwards):.

Rewrite and simplify to obtain: \(5g - T = 5a\) For \(P\) (moving upwards): \(T - 3g = 3a\) Add the equations: \(2g = 8a \Rightarrow a = \dfrac{2(9.8)}{8} = 2.45\text{ m/s}^2\) (b) Substitute \(a\) into the equation for \(P\): \(T = 3g + 3a = 3(9.8 + 2.45) = 3(12.25) = 36.75\text{ N}\).
(c) The pulley supports two vertical segments of string with tension \(T\), so the total downward force on the pulley is: \(F_{\text{pulley}} = 2T = 2(36.75)\).

question.en: A block of mass \(4\text{ kg}\) is pulled along a rough horizontal plane (\(\mu = 0.25\)) by a pulling force of magnitude \(25\text{ N}\) acting at \(30^\circ\) above the horizontal. Taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2\): (a) show that the normal reaction \(R = 26.7\text{ N}\), (b) find the acceleration of the block.

solution.en: (a) Resolve vertically (equilibrium in vertical direction): \[R + 25\sin 30^\circ = mg \Rightarrow R + 25(0.5) = 4(9.8) \Rightarrow R + 12.5 = 39.2 \Rightarrow R = 26.7\text{ N}\] (b) Limiting friction force opposes motion: \[F = \mu R = 0.25 \times 26.7 = 6.675\text{ N}\] Resolve horizontally using \(F_{\text{net}} = ma\): \[25\cos 30^\circ - F = ma \Rightarrow 25\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) - 6.675 = 4a\] \[21.651 - 6.675 = 4a \Rightarrow 14.976 = 4a \Rightarrow a = \dfrac{14.976}{4} \approx 3.74\text{ m/s}^2\text{ (3 s.f.)}\]

hints.en: (a) Resolve vertically (equilibrium in vertical direction): \(R + 25\sin 30^\circ = mg \Rightarrow R + 25(0.5) = 4(9.8) \Rightarrow R + 12.5 = 39.2 \Rightarrow R\).

(b) Limiting friction force opposes motion: \(F = \mu R = 0.25 \times 26.7 = 6.675\text{ N}\) Resolve horizontally using \(F_{\text{net}} = ma\): \(25\cos 30^\circ - F = ma \Rightarrow 25\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) - 6.675 = 4a\).
Use the resulting form to finish: \(21.651 - 6.675 = 4a \implies 14.976 = 4a \implies a = \dfrac{14.976}{4} = 3.74\text{ m/s}^2\text{ (3 s.f.)}\).

question.en: [Practice 3 · Hard] A particle of mass \(2 \text{ kg}\) is acted upon by a constant force \(\mathbf{F}\). At time \(t=0\), the particle is at the origin \((0,0)\) and has velocity \(\mathbf{v} = (3\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j}) \text{ m/s}\). At time \(t=2 \text{ s}\), the particle's velocity is \(\mathbf{v} = (7\mathbf{i} + 12\mathbf{j}) \text{ m/s}\). Determine the magnitude of the constant force \(\mathbf{F}\) acting on the particle.

hints.en: We are given the mass of the particle \(m = 2 \text{ kg}\).
The initial velocity at \(t=0\) is \(\mathbf{v}_0 = (2\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j}) \text{ m/s}\). The final velocity at \(t=2 \text{ s}\) is \(\mathbf{v}_f = (7\mathbf{i} + 28\mathbf{j}) \text{ m/s}\).
Therefore, the magnitude of the constant force \(F\) is \(5\sqrt{17} \text{ N}\).

solution.en:
We are given the mass of the particle \(m = 2 \text{ kg}\).
The initial velocity at \(t=0\) is \(\mathbf{v}_0 = (2\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j}) \text{ m/s}\).
The final velocity at \(t=2 \text{ s}\) is \(\mathbf{v}_f = (7\mathbf{i} + 28\mathbf{j}) \text{ m/s}\).

The change in velocity is \(\Delta \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}_f - \mathbf{v}_0\).
\(\Delta \mathbf{v} = (7\mathbf{i} + 28\mathbf{j}) - (2\mathbf{i} + 8\mathbf{j}) = (7-2)\mathbf{i} + (28-8)\mathbf{j} = 5\mathbf{i} + 20\mathbf{j} \text{ m/s}\).

The time interval is \(\Delta t = 2 \text{ s}\).

Since the force is constant, the acceleration \(\mathbf{a}\) is also constant.
We can calculate the acceleration using the formula \(\mathbf{a} = \frac{\Delta \mathbf{v}}{\Delta t}\).
\(\mathbf{a} = \frac{5\mathbf{i} + 20\mathbf{j}}{2} = \left(\frac{5}{2}\right)\mathbf{i} + \left(\frac{20}{2}\right)\mathbf{j} = 2.5\mathbf{i} + 10\mathbf{j} \text{ m/s}^2\).

According to Newton's second law of motion, the force \(\mathbf{F}\) acting on the particle is given by \(\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}\).
\(\mathbf{F} = 2 \times (2.5\mathbf{i} + 10\mathbf{j}) = (2 \times 2.5)\mathbf{i} + (2 \times 10)\mathbf{j} = 5\mathbf{i} + 20\mathbf{j} \text{ N}\).

The magnitude of the force \(\mathbf{F}\) is calculated as \(|\mathbf{F}| = \sqrt{F_x^2 + F_y^2}\).
\(|\mathbf{F}| = \sqrt{5^2 + 20^2} = \sqrt{25 + 400} = \sqrt{425}\).

To simplify \(\sqrt{425}\), we find the prime factorization of 425:
\(425 = 5 \times 85 = 5 \times 5 \times 17 = 5^2 \times 17\).

So, \(\sqrt{425} = \sqrt{5^2 \times 17} = \sqrt{5^2} \times \sqrt{17} = 5\sqrt{17}\).

Therefore, the magnitude of the constant force \(\mathbf{F}\) is \(5\sqrt{17} \text{ N}\).

Comparing this with the given choices:
Choice A: \(\frac{5\sqrt{17}}{2} \text{ N}\)
Choice B: \(5\sqrt{17} \text{ N}\)
Choice C: \(\frac{5\sqrt{2}}{2} \text{ N}\)
Choice D: \(5\sqrt{2} \text{ N}\)

Our calculated magnitude matches Choice B.
